acts.title: Text A · What the drawer holds
text: Shaun Usher has been collecting letters for years. His website has been publishing one a day since 2009, and it has now been running long enough to have become a book, and then five books.
What he has noticed is not that people have stopped writing. We have been writing more than any generation in history. What has changed is that almost none of it has been kept.

A letter had to be worth the postage stamp, so people thought before they wrote, and whoever received it had a physical object to put somewhere. Most of what Usher has published came out of a drawer, not an archive.
Nobody has been deliberately destroying anything. We have simply been deleting, one inbox at a time, and we have not noticed that we were doing it.

items.q: What is the main point of Text A?
o: We write more than ever, but almost none of it is kept

items.q: Where did most of the letters Usher published come from?
o: A drawer rather than an archive

acts.title: Text B · What the campaign wants back
text: Several internet campaigns have sprung up in an attempt to save the art of letter-writing, and one of them has been asking people to send a single handwritten letter a month.

The organizers have been surprised by who signs up. They had expected people over sixty. In fact most of those who have joined so far are under thirty, and many have said they have never received a handwritten letter in their lives.

The campaign has not made letters normal again, and it has not been trying to. What it has done is make people slow down for twenty minutes. Participants have been reporting the same thing: the hardest part is not the handwriting. It is deciding what is worth the paper.

items.s: The campaign asks people to send one handwritten letter a month.
The organizers expected most participants to be young.

The campaign claims it has made letter-writing normal again.
Participants say the difficult part is choosing what to write about.

acts.title: Present perfect: simple or continuous?
rule: Both forms connect the past to now. The difference is what you are pointing at. The simple form points at a result. The continuous form points at the activity that produced it, and at how long it has gone on.
points: have / has + past participle. A completed result, a finished quantity, or an achievement.
have / has been + -ing. Duration, a repeated or ongoing activity, and present evidence of recent activity.
know, be, belong, own and other state verbs stay simple even when the meaning is duration: I have known her for years, never “have been knowing”.
eg: She has written three letters this month.
Simple — a finished quantity. How many.
She has been writing letters all afternoon.
Continuous — duration. How long.
They have found a way of saving the archive.
Simple — a result you can point to.
They have been looking for a way for two years.
Continuous — the search itself, possibly still going on.
I have read your email.
Simple — finished. I know what it says.
I have been reading your email.
Continuous — possibly not finished, and it explains why I am slow.
Sorry about the mess — I have been sorting out the loft.
Continuous — present evidence of recent activity.
The website has been running since 2009.
Continuous with since — the classic duration pattern.
We have known each other since school.
Simple, because know is a state verb.
How long have you been waiting?
Continuous — the standard way to ask about duration.
acts.careful: “I have been writing three letters” is wrong. A finished number always takes the simple form, however long it took.

write.q: Write about your own written communication over the last few years — what you have been doing, and what you have actually finished or kept. Use the continuous form at least three times for activities and duration, and the simple form at least three times for results and finished quantities.
plan: what you have finished or kept (simple)
one thing you have been meaning to do
what you still have not done
write.model: Over the last few years I have been writing more than at any point in my life, and almost none of it exists any more. I have sent something like forty thousand messages since I started this job. I have kept nine. My grandmother has kept every letter she has received since 1962; they are in a drawer that has not closed properly for a decade. I have been meaning to write to her properly since March. I have already bought the paper, which probably tells you how serious I am. I still have not written a word, and the honest reason is not time. It is that a message costs nothing and a letter has to be worth the stamp.
